metadata.name: find
metadata.displayName: find - Search for files and directories
metadata.description: Search for files and directories in a directory hierarchy

installation.note: find is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: find is a powerful command-line utility for searching files and directories in a directory hierarchy. It can search by name, type, size, modification time, permissions, and many other criteria. Unlike ls, find can recursively search through all subdirectories.
when_to_use: Search for files by name across the entire directory tree
Find files matching specific criteria (size, date, permissions)
Locate files that were modified recently or are larger than a certain size
Find and perform actions on files (delete, move, execute commands)
Search for files by type (regular files, directories, symlinks)
Locate files based on complex combinations of criteria

misconceptions.title: find searches only the current directory
misconceptions.misconception: find only looks in the current directory like ls
misconceptions.reality: find recursively searches all subdirectories by default. If you want to search only the current directory, use -maxdepth 0 or -maxdepth 1.
misconceptions.tip: Remember: find is recursive. Use -maxdepth to limit search depth.

misconceptions.title: find requires wildcards in -name
misconceptions.misconception: You must always use wildcards (*, ?) with -name
misconceptions.reality: You can search for exact names: find . -name 'myfile.txt'. Wildcards are optional and only needed when searching for patterns.
misconceptions.tip: Exact match: find . -name 'exact.txt'. Pattern match: find . -name '*.txt'

misconceptions.title: -size uses exact bytes
misconceptions.reality: -size works with 512-byte blocks internally. +100M means larger than 100MB (approximately), not exactly 100MB. The calculation is approximate due to block rounding.
misconceptions.tip: Use -size +100M to find files larger than 100MB. Exact sizes are not possible due to block allocation.

misconceptions.title: -mtime -1 means within the last hour
misconceptions.misconception: -mtime -1 means files modified in the last hour
misconceptions.reality: -mtime works in 24-hour periods. -mtime -1 means modified within the last 24 hours, not the last hour. Use -mmin for minute-based searches.
misconceptions.tip: Days: -mtime. Minutes: -mmin. -mtime -1 = last 24 hours, -mmin -60 = last hour

misconceptions.title: find is slow
misconceptions.misconception: find is always slow because it searches everything
misconceptions.reality: find can be fast if you use appropriate criteria and limits. Use -maxdepth to limit depth, start from specific directories, and combine criteria effectively. For simple filename searches, locate may be faster.
misconceptions.tip: Start from specific directories, use -maxdepth when possible, and combine multiple criteria to narrow results quickly

common_pitfalls.description: Wildcards (*, ?, []) are expanded by the shell before find sees them
common_pitfalls.solution: Always quote patterns: find . -name "*.txt" not find . -name *.txt. Unquoted wildcards may match files in the current directory unexpectedly.

common_pitfalls.description: Using -delete without first checking what will be deleted
common_pitfalls.solution: Always test first: find . -name "*.tmp" -print. Review the output, then use -delete. Never combine -delete with -exec rm {} \; (redundant and dangerous).

common_pitfalls.description: Forgetting to escape the semicolon or space in -exec commands
common_pitfalls.solution: Use \; (backslash-semicolon) to terminate -exec commands. There must be a space before \;. Alternatively, use -exec with + for better performance.
Remember: - means less than (recent), + means more than (old). -mtime -7 = within last 7 days, -mtime +30 = older than 30 days.

common_pitfalls.description: Forgetting to specify a starting directory searches from current directory, or accidentally searching from /
common_pitfalls.solution: Always specify the starting directory explicitly. Use . for current directory, ~ for home, or absolute paths. Avoid find / unless you specifically need to search the entire system.
common_pitfalls.performance: Searching from / can take a very long time and may search protected system directories.

best_practices: Always quote wildcard patterns to prevent shell expansion: find . -name "*.txt"
Test find commands with -print or -ls before using -delete or -exec with destructive commands
Use -type f when searching for files (excludes directories unless you specifically want them)
Specify starting directory explicitly: use . (current), ~ (home), or absolute paths
Use -maxdepth to limit search depth when you don't need deep recursion (faster searches)
Combine criteria effectively to narrow results before performing actions
Use -exec with + instead of \; when processing many files (more efficient): find . -name "*.txt" -exec rm {} +
Use locate for simple filename searches (if updatedb is maintained) - it's much faster
Quote or escape special characters in patterns and filenames
Check file permissions before deleting - use -ls first to see ownership and permissions
performance_tips: Start from the most specific directory possible (don't search / if you only need /home)
Use -maxdepth to limit recursion depth - searching only 2-3 levels deep is much faster
Put most selective criteria first (e.g., -name before -type) - find evaluates left to right
Use locate instead of find for simple filename searches if the database is up to date
Avoid searching network filesystems or very large directory trees if possible
Use -exec with + (plus) instead of \; (semicolon) - processes multiple files per command invocation
Combine -prune with -name to skip entire subdirectories (advanced optimization)

additional_notes.operators_precedence: Logical operators precedence: ( ) > ! > -a (AND) > -o (OR). Use parentheses for clarity.
additional_notes.exec_vs_xargs: -exec {} \; runs command once per file. -exec {} + or xargs batches files together (more efficient for many files).
additional_notes.permissions: You can only find files in directories you have permission to read. Use sudo find if you need to search system directories.
additional_notes.symlinks: By default, find follows symlinks. Use -P to never follow, -L to always follow, -H to follow only on command line arguments.

complex_examples.find_not_owned: find /home -type f ! -user $(whoami) (files not owned by current user)

additional_notes.safety_reminder: Always verify find results with -print or -ls before using -delete or destructive -exec commands. Test on a small subset first.
